title: Revising the Teacher Affiliative Practices Scale (TAP‐S): Development and Validation of General and Specific Student‐Reported Versions in Secondary Education
text_snippet: Revising the Teacher Affiliative Practices Scale (TAP‐S): Development and Validation of General and Specific Student‐Reported Versions in Secondary Education ABSTRACT Current measures of teacher−student relationships (TSRs) often emphasize relational constructs (e.g., trust, liking) but overlook specific teacher behaviors that foster these relationships. In particular, there is limited research on how TSRs are built and maintained in secondary education. One notable exception is the newly developed Teacher Affiliative Practices−Student Perspective (TAP‐S), an instrument designed to assess students' perceptions of teachers' everyday relationship‐building and relationship‐maintaining practices in secondary schools. Given the scale's limitations, the purpose of this study was to refine the TAP‐S and further evaluate the psychometric properties of the revised instrument in both its general form (assessing perceptions of teachers in general) and its specific form (assessing perceptions of one particular teacher). A total of 393 secondary school students participated ( M age = 12.71 years, SD = 0.68; 52.7% boys), all from the 7th and 8th grade of secondary education. title: Beyond Replacement: Episode‐Based Pathways Between Generative AI and School Counselor Help‐Seeking Among Indonesian Adolescents
text_snippet: Beyond Replacement: Episode‐Based Pathways Between Generative AI and School Counselor Help‐Seeking Among Indonesian Adolescents ABSTRACT Adolescents use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for emotional support, yet little is known about how GenAI and school counselors are used within the same problem episode. This explanatory sequential mixed methods study examined 432 Indonesian students aged 15–18 years; 192 (44.4%) had used GenAI for personal or emotional problems in the previous 6 months. Among these students, 124 (64.6%) involved human support within the same episode. Five pathways were identified: GenAI only (35.4%), GenAI → non‐school‐based human support (25.5%), GenAI → school counselor (22.4%), parallel use (11.5%), and school counselor → GenAI (5.2%). Psychological distress was not associated with counselor involvement. title: What Does It Look Like to Evaluate “Handle Frustration Well”? Measurement Invariance of the Devereux Early Childhood Assessment Across Gender, Race/Ethnicity, and Home Language
text_snippet: What Does It Look Like to Evaluate “Handle Frustration Well”? Measurement Invariance of the Devereux Early Childhood Assessment Across Gender, Race/Ethnicity, and Home Language ABSTRACT The Devereux Early Childhood Assessment (DECA) is a measure of children's positive social‐emotional functioning. This study aimed to validate the factor structure of DECA and test measurement invariance across different demographic groups. Secondary data analysis was conducted using data from one Head Start program, employing a multi‐stage sampling approach. DECA scores from 1209 children were used to test for measurement invariance. While one item of the DECA had to be dropped due to low factor loadings, the original 3‐factor structure of the DECA was supported. Additionally, measurement invariance was found across gender, race/ethnicity, and home language status. The study's findings support the DECA as a valid and reliable tool for assessing social and emotional development in diverse populations, with implications for research and practice in early childhood assessment.

title: Bullying Victimization across Chinese Urban and Rural Adolescents: Measurement Invariance and Network Analysis
text_snippet: Bullying Victimization across Chinese Urban and Rural Adolescents: Measurement Invariance and Network Analysis ABSTRACT This study aimed to (1) examine measurement invariance of the Delaware Bullying Victimization Scale‐Student (DBVS‐S) between adolescents recruited from one urban and one rural middle school in China and (2) use network analysis to examine item features of the DBVS‐S across samples and identify network differences. A total of 4,527 students were included, comprising 2,074 Chinese urban (44.89% boys and 55.11% girls; M age = 16.42 years, SD = 0.80 years) and 2,453 rural (49.86% boys and 50.14% girls; M age = 16.73 years, SD = 1.02 years) adolescents. Results of multi‐group confirmatory factor analysis showed that bullying victimization achieved partial scalar invariance. Adolescents in the sampled rural school reported higher levels of verbal, physical, and relational bullying victimization than those in the sampled urban school. Results of network analysis revealed that verbal and physical bullying victimization was at the center of the urban sample's network, whereas relational bullying was at the center of the rural sample's network. title: Faculty Diversity and Preparedness in School Psychology Among Early‐Career Scholars in the United States
text_snippet: Faculty Diversity and Preparedness in School Psychology Among Early‐Career Scholars in the United States ABSTRACT School psychology faces persistent shortages of practitioners and faculty, raising concerns about the profession's capacity to meet students’ growing academic, behavioral, and mental health needs. This study surveyed 40 early‐career school psychology faculty across the United States to examine demographic characteristics, training pathways, scholarly productivity, preparedness, and satisfaction. Participants completed an online survey with demographic, professional, and career‐related questions, as well as open‐ended items exploring factors that promoted or hindered pursuit of academic careers. Participants represented a range of racial, ethnic, linguistic, and disability identities, with 55% identifying as Black, Indigenous, or People of Color (BIPOC), 22.5% reporting fluency in a language other than English, and 20% identifying as having a dis/ability. Most participants reported satisfaction with their positions and received a job offer during their first faculty search. Faculty who completed postdoctoral training reported significantly higher preparedness than those who did not. title: Roots and Consequences of Teacher Isolation: A Data‐Driven Study of Language Teachers' Perceptions in an EFL Context
text_snippet: Roots and Consequences of Teacher Isolation: A Data‐Driven Study of Language Teachers' Perceptions in an EFL Context ABSTRACT The comparative effect of teaching in isolation or collaboration with others has been extensively explored. Still, more often than not, these studies are theory‐driven and, as such, give teachers' perspectives very little voice. While recent scholarship has begun to explore teacher isolation more comprehensively (Flores 2020), this data‐driven study aims to fill remaining gaps by exploring the roots and consequences of teacher isolation from the bottom up. To this end, 15 language teachers working in private language schools in Shahrood, a major city in Semnan Province, Iran, were purposively sampled, and their concerns and perspectives were collected and conceptualized in line with grounded theory (Corbin and Strauss 2008). Iterative data collection and analysis yielded language teacher isolation as the core category, related to factors such as tight schedules, a lack of shared concerns with other teachers, a judgmental workplace atmosphere, overwork, and egotism. The consequences of teaching in isolation were the routinization of practice and the atrophy of language‐teaching skills. title: Examining Teacher Factors Related to Disproportionate Discipline for Soft Offenses: An Analysis Examining Teacher Perceptions
text_snippet: Examining Teacher Factors Related to Disproportionate Discipline for Soft Offenses: An Analysis Examining Teacher Perceptions ABSTRACT Teachers' culturally responsive practices and wellbeing have been theorized as relevant to racial disparities in exclusionary discipline, but empirical research examining these associations is limited. Using state administrative data and teacher survey reports from 23 middle schools and 574 teachers, this study examined whether school‐level disproportionality in out‐of‐school suspensions, particularly for soft offenses, was associated with teacher‐reported use of culturally responsive practices (CRPs), multicultural teaching self‐efficacy, stress, and burnout. Specifically, we used linear regression models with cluster‐robust standard errors to account for clustering to examine associations between school‐level disproportionality metrics and teacher‐reported outcomes. Results indicated that school‐level disproportionality was not associated with teachers' self‐reported use of CRPs. However, greater disproportionality, particularly for all offenses, was associated with lower multicultural teaching self‐efficacy and higher teacher stress; associations with burnout were weaker and less consistent. title: Unveiling Universal Mental Health Screening: School Psychologists' Perspectives & Practices
text_snippet: Unveiling Universal Mental Health Screening: School Psychologists' Perspectives & Practices ABSTRACT The critical need to address mental health problems among children, combined with the increasing emphasis on universal mental health screening in school settings, underscores the importance of understanding influences on the use of these measures. There is a mental health crisis in the nation, yet the use of universal mental health screening varies across the country. This study examined how school psychologists use universal screening tools in their work to understand variability in their use across schools. Using a survey design, the researchers developed and administered a survey to school psychologists to gather perceptions and insights regarding the implementation and use of universal screening measures. Questions focused on school psychologists' use of universal screening tools for behavioral and mental health, including both contextual and personal factors that may influence the use of universal social‐emotional screeners. The findings identified significant predictors of screening and revealed national trends in the use of these tools. Implications for practice and recommendations for future research are discussed.

title: Ethical Practice Under Constraint: Structural Barriers and Professional Decision‐Making Among School Psychologists in Greece
text_snippet: Ethical Practice Under Constraint: Structural Barriers and Professional Decision‐Making Among School Psychologists in Greece ABSTRACT School psychologists frequently encounter ethically challenging professional practices shaped not only by professional responsibilities but also by structural conditions within educational systems. This study examined ethical preparedness and perceived ethical challenges among school psychologists working in public schools in Greece, with particular attention to organizational and professional factors. A total of 355 school psychologists completed a structured questionnaire assessing ethical preparedness, frequency of ethical dilemmas, supervision experiences, working conditions, and perceived structural barriers. Hierarchical regression and mediation analyses were conducted to examine relationships among these variables. Results indicated that structural constraints—such as temporary employment, limited resources, and lack of dedicated workspace—were significantly associated with greater ethical challenges in professional practice. Supervision and perceived ethical preparedness were associated with more confident ethical decision‐making but did not mediate the effects of structural conditions. title: Psychosocial Profiles of Tanzanian Primary School Children and Their Associations With School Refusal, Absenteeism, and Academic Performance
text_snippet: Psychosocial Profiles of Tanzanian Primary School Children and Their Associations With School Refusal, Absenteeism, and Academic Performance ABSTRACT This study examined psychosocial profiles of Tanzanian primary school children and their associations with school refusal, absenteeism, and academic performance using a person‐centered approach. Guided primarily by Bronfenbrenner's bioecological PPCT model, and secondarily by Kearney's functional model of school refusal, school functioning was conceptualised as shaped by child vulnerabilities and proximal relational contexts. Participants were 496 pupils (58.6% female, 41.4% male; ages 9–15 years, M = 11.97, SD = 1.28) from Grades 4–7 in 10 government primary schools. Gaussian finite mixture modeling supported a six‐profile solution based on separation anxiety, externalising and attention symptoms, and perceived parent and peer support. Multilevel analyses accounting for school‐level clustering showed no statistically significant overall profile differences in absenteeism or academic performance. title: Evaluating the Reliability, Structure, and Measurement Invariance of the Panorama Student Survey in Middle School
text_snippet: Evaluating the Reliability, Structure, and Measurement Invariance of the Panorama Student Survey in Middle School ABSTRACT Student perception surveys are increasingly used to inform school improvement efforts, yet evidence regarding their psychometric properties remains limited in many applied contexts. The present study examined the reliability, temporal stability, and measurement structure of the Panorama Student Survey in a large sample of middle school students. Data were drawn from 18,020 survey administrations across Fall 2022 and Spring 2023, representing 10,196 unique students in Grades 6–8. Internal consistency reliability, test–retest stability, and confirmatory factor analyses were conducted to evaluate the measurement structure of the survey domains. Results indicated strong internal consistency across constructs ( α = 0.68–0.86; ω = 0.81–0.92) and moderate to strong temporal stability across waves ( r = 0.58–0.70). title: Examining the Relationship Between Bullying and Extracurricular Involvement
text_snippet: Examining the Relationship Between Bullying and Extracurricular Involvement ABSTRACT Bullying involvement (e.g., perpetration, victimization, relational, physical) is pervasive both within school and in out‐of‐school environments (Musu‐Gillette et al., 2018). Few studies have examined the relationship between gender, bullying, and participation in extracurricular activities; however, extracurricular involvement is a predictor of multiple positive student outcomes (Berger et al., 2020; Camp, 1990; Peguero, 2008). This study aims to examine bullying and extracurricular involvement by gender, as well as assess whether there is a relationship between extracurricular activities and bullying involvement. From a survey of 14,508 secondary students within the United States, results indicated that males reported higher rates of bullying perpetration, relational perpetration, physical aggression, and victimization, whereas females reported higher rates of relational victimization. Findings relating to gender, extracurricular involvement, limitations, and implications for practice are discussed.

title: Evaluating IEP Goals Addressing Social, Emotional, and Behavioral Health in Autistic Middle Schoolers
text_snippet: Evaluating IEP Goals Addressing Social, Emotional, and Behavioral Health in Autistic Middle Schoolers ABSTRACT Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) are the mechanism through which students receive special education services in schools. Little is known about the degree to which federal guidelines and science‐based recommendations are evident in IEPs for autistic students, particularly those targeting social‐emotional and behavioral health in middle school. Given the centrality of social‐emotional and behavioral health in shaping academic success, it is critical to understand how these needs are addressed via IEPs. This study examined the quality of IEPs for 50 autistic students enrolled in grades 6 through 8, including how IEP goals related to social‐emotional and behavioral health reflected quality standards established in the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act of 2006 and the National Research Council. Of 347 IEP objectives, just under half (42%) targeted social‐emotional and behavioral health‐related outcomes. Analysis of IEP quality indicated moderate adherence to legal standards and best practice recommendations, with variation across individual indicators of quality. title: Individual and Professional Factors Associated With Teacher Emotional Exhaustion, Stress, Coping, and Self‐Efficacy Across Four Nations
text_snippet: Individual and Professional Factors Associated With Teacher Emotional Exhaustion, Stress, Coping, and Self‐Efficacy Across Four Nations ABSTRACT We surveyed 1223 teachers from Iran, Japan, Türkiye, and the US to examine the relations among individual and professional factors and teacher emotional exhaustion, stress, coping, and self‐efficacy. Teachers in all four countries reported high levels of stress, moderate levels of emotional exhaustion and coping, and moderate‐to‐high levels of self‐efficacy. Stress and coping emerged as the strongest predictors of both emotional exhaustion and attrition risk across nations, while self‐efficacy served an important protective role. A substantial proportion of teachers were found to be at risk of leaving the profession. These results underscore the urgent need for interventions to promote teacher well‐being, especially in US schools and special education teachers, who were identified as being particularly vulnerable. Given the profound impact of teacher well‐being on instructional quality, student outcomes, and the sustainability of the teaching workforce, addressing these risks constitutes a non‐negotiable priority for educational policy.

title: School‐Based Educational Involvement for Families With a History of Parental Incarceration: A Systematic Review
text_snippet: School‐Based Educational Involvement for Families With a History of Parental Incarceration: A Systematic Review ABSTRACT An estimated 5.1 million children in the United States have experienced parental incarceration (Annie E. Casey Foundation 2016). Only recently has research begun considering protective factors in mitigating negative school‐based outcomes associated with this experience. Parental educational involvement is a critical factor in student outcomes, yet there is a gap in research regarding its role for underrepresented student populations, particularly those affected by parental incarceration. This systematic review addresses this gap by evaluating the nature of school‐based educational involvement for families affected by parental incarceration and by investigating the barriers and facilitators to that involvement. Our review of seven studies revealed mixed evidence. We identified key takeaways: parenting and literacy programs have the potential to facilitate involvement, family narratives are crucial to understanding engagement, and there is a need for further studies that disaggregate between maternal and paternal incarceration. title: Reliability, Validity, and Acceptability of the Scope Classroom Observation Code (SCOC) to Identify Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)‐Related Behaviours in UK Primary Schools
text_snippet: Reliability, Validity, and Acceptability of the Scope Classroom Observation Code (SCOC) to Identify Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)‐Related Behaviours in UK Primary Schools ABSTRACT ADHD is a prevalent disorder that impacts academic and social functioning in childhood. Teachers often struggle to identify ADHD. This study evaluated the Scope Classroom Observation Checklist's (SCOC) reliability, validity, and acceptability as a potential screening measure for school staff to identify ADHD characteristics. Parents and teachers completed the Attention‐Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Rating Scale‐5 (ADHD‐RS‐5). Those who scored ≥ 75th percentile by both raters were considered ‘high symptom’ and were assessed with the reference standard: Section J of the Development and Wellbeing Assessment (DAWBA). Based on the measures, children were split into 3 groups: high‐probability ADHD, intermediate‐probability ADHD and no‐ADHD. 420 children were observed with the SCOC, yielding on/off‐task and hyperactive/impulsive scores. Inter‐rater reliability (IRR) on the SCOC was quantified using the intra‐class correlation coefficient (ICC). The area under the curve (AUC) was used to quantify the ability of the SCOC to discriminate children with high‐probability ADHD from those without; intermediate‐ from high‐probability ADHD and high symptom ADHD from no ADHD. title: Sources of Strength for School‐Based Suicide Prevention: Key Implementation Strategies Based on School Professional Perspectives
text_snippet: Sources of Strength for School‐Based Suicide Prevention: Key Implementation Strategies Based on School Professional Perspectives ABSTRACT As concerns for rising rates of youth suicide and suicidal thoughts and behaviors continue to grow, there is a need to prioritize school‐based suicide prevention programs. Despite evidence documenting the effectiveness of school‐based prevention programs for reducing suicide‐related risk in adolescents, schools face numerous barriers to successfully implementing programs with fidelity. Therefore, the present study aimed to identify tailored implementation strategies to increase fidelity and sustainability of school‐based suicide prevention programs. We first used focus groups to explore school personnel ( N = 16) perspectives on barriers and facilitators of the implementation of Sources of Strength , an evidence‐based suicide prevention program. Next, we conducted a co‐design session with nine of these participants to identify actionable implementation strategies based on school personnel input. Last, to translate findings into practice, we developed an implementation toolkit to support delivery of Sources of Strength and other upstream suicide prevention programs. title: Transitioning to Higher Education: A Case Study of an Individual With Autism
text_snippet: Transitioning to Higher Education: A Case Study of an Individual With Autism ABSTRACT Necessary arrangements should be made to enable university students with autism (the term “autism” is used to refer to the entire autism spectrum in this study) to improve their transition to university. The need for support may be higher in countries like Türkiye, where the number of university students with autism is relatively low, as universities have limited experience with these students. Thus, this study focuses on the transition process of an individual with autism to higher education in Türkiye. It aims to contribute to the transition processes of the student and, accordingly, of future students with autism. In this qualitative case study, data were collected through semi‐structured interviews with an individual with autism and members of his close circle during his transition to higher education. The study involved 29 participants: the university student with autism, two family members, eight high school teachers, eight university lecturers, and ten university classmates. title: The Effects of Tootling on Complimenting and Peer Prompting in Second‐Grade Students
text_snippet: The Effects of Tootling on Complimenting and Peer Prompting in Second‐Grade Students ABSTRACT Tootling interventions can enhance students' social skill performance outside the social skill training environment. With Tootling interventions, group‐oriented rewards are delivered contingent upon the number of reports students provide of their peers' engagement in prosocial behavior(s). An A‐B‐A‐B withdrawal design was used to evaluate the effects of Tootling on complimenting peers and peer prompting as a group of five second‐grade students played a math game. Visual and effect‐size analyses of our data showed higher rates of complimenting and peer‐prompting when the Tootling intervention was applied. Across intervention sessions, complimenting and peer prompting were positively correlated, and this correlation was statistically significant. These results extend previous research and suggest that positive peer mediation (e.g., prompting) may partially explain why Tootling interventions increase students' performance of recently trained social skills. The discussion focuses on future research designed to enhance the impact of Tootling interventions, positive peer mediation, and students' social skill development.

title: Small Group Instruction Can Improve Adolescent Mental Health and Peer Relations: Findings From A Technology‐Assisted Cooperative Learning Intervention
text_snippet: Small Group Instruction Can Improve Adolescent Mental Health and Peer Relations: Findings From A Technology‐Assisted Cooperative Learning Intervention ABSTRACT Internalizing symptoms in adolescents (e.g., anxiety, loneliness, depression) increased following the COVID‐19 pandemic, and can have detrimental impacts on engagement, learning, and overall school success. Cooperative Learning (CL), a small‐group instructional approach that creates intergroup collaboration among students, has an extensive track record of improving peer relations and school belonging, which may reduce social stress and protect against internalizing symptoms. However, adhering to the key design principles that make CL successful can be difficult for teachers to do in their everyday practice, underscoring the need for technology‐assisted CL. This study evaluated the first‐year outcomes of a universal, technology‐assisted CL intervention (i.e., PeerLearning. net) on peer relations and, in turn, internalizing symptoms. We also examined whether intervention effects varied by students’ baseline symptom levels, sex, and race. title: The Effects of PLUSS: Adapting an Evidence‐Based Reading Intervention for Multilingual Learners
text_snippet: The Effects of PLUSS: Adapting an Evidence‐Based Reading Intervention for Multilingual Learners ABSTRACT The effects of an evidence‐based literacy intervention with and without added supports to address the unique needs of multilingual learners (MLs) were assessed through an ABAB single‐case withdrawal design. The dual dependent variables were reading fluency/accuracy and performance on the workbook that included spelling, vocabulary, and reading comprehension tasks. Three students (one each in second, third, and fourth grades) who qualified for English language development services and exhibited low reading performance (second and third graders) or were identified with a reading disability (fourth grader) participated. From the initial baseline phase (A1) to the final intervention phase (B2), adding supports specific to the unique language needs of these MLs was associated with increases in reading fluency, decoding accuracy, and workbook performance (measure of reading comprehension, vocabulary knowledge, and decoding/spelling). title: Student Recognition and Bystander Behaviors in School Bullying: A Random Intercept Cross‐Lagged Panel Model
text_snippet: Student Recognition and Bystander Behaviors in School Bullying: A Random Intercept Cross‐Lagged Panel Model ABSTRACT Passive bystanding and active defending are distinct responses to school bullying, yet the role of student recognition in driving these behaviors remains unclear. This study employed a three‐wave longitudinal research design with a sample of 314 students to disentangle stable between‐person effects from dynamic within‐person effects through a Random Intercept Cross‐Lagged Panel Model (RI‐CLPM). The results revealed a significant divergence in how recognition is associated with the two bystander behaviors. At the within‐person level, recognition significantly and positively predicted subsequent active defending; however, recognition did not significantly reduce passive bystanding at this level. At the between‐person level, students who generally experienced higher levels of recognition across the year reported significantly lower levels of passive bystanding, whereas the link to defending was not significant.

title: Examining Parent, Teacher, School Mental Health Professional, and Researcher Perceptions of a Tier 2 Internalizing Intervention to Promote Feasibility, Usability, and Effectiveness
text_snippet: Examining Parent, Teacher, School Mental Health Professional, and Researcher Perceptions of a Tier 2 Internalizing Intervention to Promote Feasibility, Usability, and Effectiveness ABSTRACT The purpose of this study was to inform the continued development and refinement of the Resilience Education Program (REP), a Tier 2 targeted intervention for students in grades 4–8 exhibiting early signs of internalizing problems. Parents ( n = 7), teachers ( n = 7), school mental health professionals ( n = 11), and researchers ( n = 6) participated in focus groups to provide feedback on the REP intervention. During focus groups, we used a modified nominal group technique to elicit participant feedback regarding REP feasibility, usability, and potential effectiveness. We used qualitative analysis to identify major and minor thematic categories in participant responses. We identified 7 major and 17 minor categories for parent perceptions of REP. For the teacher, school mental health professional, and researcher perceptions about REP, we identified 8 major and 20 minor categories. Categories addressed REP's strengths and limitations, implementation considerations, and strategies to increase engagement. title: Advancing a National Dialogue on Disability in Catholic Education
text_snippet: Advancing a National Dialogue on Disability in Catholic Education ABSTRACT This qualitative descriptive study examined perspectives from 85 participants at the National Convening on Disability and Catholic Education, a 3‐day gathering of Catholic school leaders, educators, and advocates. Using reflexive thematic analysis of structured roundtable dialogues, the study identified psychological and organizational factors influencing inclusive practice in faith‐based school contexts. Five interrelated themes emerged: (a) the need for a coherent, nationally aligned inclusion framework; (b) educator beliefs and fear as determinants of implementation; (c) fragmentation across school and diocesan systems; (d) procedural barriers related to IDEA proportionate share; and (e) belonging as a central student outcome. Findings suggest that sustainable inclusion depends on the interaction of educator mindset, organizational coherence, and coordinated leadership structures. Implications include the importance of psychological safety, role clarity, and systems alignment when implementing inclusive practices in private school settings. title: Supporting Students on the Right PATH in Catholic Schools
text_snippet: Supporting Students on the Right PATH in Catholic Schools ABSTRACT Low‐income, first‐generation students can benefit from programs designed to reduce the college access opportunity gap. This paper describes the PATH program, operating in two Catholic grade schools in the Southwest in partnership with the University of Notre Dame. The PATH program includes a 5‐week summer experience and a course during the school year for each of the years in grades 6–8 focused on developing noncognitive skills. Surveys administered at the end of the summer experience and at the end of each school year showed that students perceive improved perseverance, school valuation, study skills, and sense of efficacy. Findings are consistent with the conceptual model of the program based on expectancy‐value theory of motivation.

title: Thriving in School‐Age Youth: A Latent Profile Analysis of Social‐Emotional Adjustment, Prosocial Behavior, and Academic Competence
text_snippet: Thriving in School‐Age Youth: A Latent Profile Analysis of Social‐Emotional Adjustment, Prosocial Behavior, and Academic Competence ABSTRACT The Positive Youth Development (PYD) framework highlights that all youth have the potential to thrive, though the expression and development of their strengths can differ significantly. Recognizing these individual differences is critical for designing effective interventions that help youth apply their strengths to meet developmental demands. This study investigated the variability in three PYD‐related strengths: social‐emotional adjustment, prosocial behavior, and academic competence. The sample consisted of 1719 school‐age youth from Grades 1 to 12 (ages 6–17), drawn from Wave 1 of the second National Survey of Child and Adolescent Well‐Being (NSCAW‐II). Latent Profile Analysis was conducted using seven key indicators. Four distinct profiles were identified: Social‐Emotional‐Behavioral Vulnerable (20%), Academically Struggling (16%), Academically Competent with Emotional‐Behavioral Challenged (36%), and Well‐Functioning (28%). These profiles reflect diverse patterns of strengths and challenges across PYD domains, highlighting the need for tailored support strategies—particularly those aimed at strengthening social and emotional competencies.

title: A Systematic Review of School Connectedness in Middle School Students
text_snippet: A Systematic Review of School Connectedness in Middle School Students ABSTRACT School connectedness has been studied in a variety of contexts and demographics and is linked to academic achievement, mental health outcomes, and overall wellbeing. In this systematic review, we identify and analyze factors associated with school connectedness among middle school students to synthesize the field's current knowledge on school connectedness and highlight future directions. Following PRISMA guidelines, we reviewed peer‐reviewed studies published between 2014 and 2025 identified through PsycINFO, PsycArticles, and ERIC. Inclusion criteria required studies to focus on middle school populations (grades 6–8) and examine predictors, correlates, or barriers to school connectedness. A total of 49 studies met inclusion criteria. Factors positively associated with school connectedness included academic engagement, supportive relationships with teachers and peers, and indicators of emotional well‐being. In contrast, barriers to school connectedness included experiences of discrimination, peer victimization, and mental health difficulties. title: Advancing Neuro‐Affirming Practices in Christian K‐12 Schools: A Neuro‐Inclusive Critical Disability Theology Framework
text_snippet: Advancing Neuro‐Affirming Practices in Christian K‐12 Schools: A Neuro‐Inclusive Critical Disability Theology Framework ABSTRACT For centuries, faith‐based education has been woven into the moral fabric of our society. It has been marked as a sacred vocation that embraces a commitment to the holistic development of all those who are in greater need of support. However, despite the notable increase in prevalence of autism spectrum disorder in recent times, K‐12 Christian schools have focused limited attention on creating supportive and neuro‐inclusive experiences for their rising number of Autistic learners. This conceptual paper seeks to stimulate improved neuro‐affirming practices at Christian K‐12 schools. It introduces a Neuro‐Inclusive Critical Disability Theology (NICDT) framework of practice for educators, school psychologists, policymakers, and faith leaders (including clergy) who support neurodiverse students enrolled at Christian K‐12 schools. The NICDT framework is grounded in Disability Theology, Critical Disability Theory, and Conjoint Behavioral Consultation. title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Strengthen MTSS Within Catholic Schools
text_snippet: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Strengthen MTSS Within Catholic Schools ABSTRACT Many Catholic schools face resource challenges that result in limitations surrounding the implementation of multi‐tiered systems and support (MTSS). Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a potential tool for Catholic schools to strengthen systems of support. This article provides a conceptual analysis regarding opportunities for AI to strengthen core components of MTSS, such as identifying evidence‐based interventions, developing progress monitoring tools, analyzing student data, and facilitating personalized instruction. The article also discusses the challenges and limitations of leveraging AI within Catholic schools, specifically when supporting staff and students. Although the article is focused on US contexts, there are conceptual implications that may extend to Catholic schools' systems internationally, specifically related to strengthening the mission of Catholic education. Future researchers should consider evaluating and analyzing the implementation of AI tools within MTSS, specifically how AI tools may support Catholic schools with resource limitations, time constraints, and expertise barriers.

title: Living Well With Type 1 Diabetes in Middle School: A Student‐Centered Perspective
text_snippet: Living Well With Type 1 Diabetes in Middle School: A Student‐Centered Perspective ABSTRACT Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is among the most common chronic illnesses affecting children and adolescents, meaning that all schools regularly include students with T1D. Supporting their well‐being requires understanding how they experience middle school to address their specific needs. This qualitative, child‐centered study, grounded in principles of grounded theory, explored the school experiences of 25 middle school students aged 11–15 living with T1D in France, using semi‐structured interviews. Analysis revealed several key dimensions shaping their experience. A prominent theme was their desire to go through school “like everyone else” despite the constraints of the illness. This aspiration led to two central needs: a well‐informed social environment and discreet attentiveness from teachers. Several levers for creating a supportive school environment emerged from the findings: rethinking technological devices to better fit school constraints; providing targeted information and training to school staff; raising awareness among all students to democratize knowledge about the condition; and fostering a professional attitude that combines understanding with discretion.

title: Video Peer Modeling in K‐12 Settings: A Research Synthesis
text_snippet: Video Peer Modeling in K‐12 Settings: A Research Synthesis ABSTRACT Many barriers to effective evidence‐based intervention implementation exist in K–12 settings, especially the lack of time and resources, highlighting the need for effective and feasible interventions. Despite its promising effectiveness and feasibility advantages, video peer modeling to date has not been systematically reviewed to provide evidence‐based guidance for school practitioners and researchers. The present study fills this gap by reviewing extant empirical studies that examined video peer modeling applied in K–12 settings. Thirty studies that met the inclusion criteria were summarized by their (a) intervention dosage, (b) intervention components, (c) target skill areas, (d) skill‐specific effectiveness, and (e) methodological quality. Results suggest that video peer modeling typically involves several components in addition to video‐viewing, including verbal reinforcement, tangible reinforcement, prompting, explicit instruction, feedback, self‐monitoring, and visual aids. Results also suggest that, across academic, social‐emotional‐behavioral, and adaptive domains, video peer modeling shows promising effectiveness in improving a wide range of skills in schools.

title: A Dual Country Validation of the Basic Psychological Needs Satisfaction and Frustration Scale: A New Focus on School Relationships
text_snippet: A Dual Country Validation of the Basic Psychological Needs Satisfaction and Frustration Scale: A New Focus on School Relationships ABSTRACT Despite the growing interest in basic psychological needs within educational settings, existing measures fail to distinguish between students' relationships with teachers and classmates, limiting the understanding of how different social dynamics uniquely impact need satisfaction and frustration during adolescence. This study provided psychometric evidence for a refined school‐specific version of the Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction and Frustration Scale (BPNSFS), while also assessing differences in the satisfaction and frustration of psychological needs between early adolescents and adolescents, in Italy and the United Kingdom. A total of 1523 students (49.6% female; mean age = 12.84) completed the refined BPNSFS, specifically designed to separately measure dimensions of relatedness with classmates and teachers. title: Better Together: Peer Coaching to Strengthen Autism Support in Rural Schools
text_snippet: Better Together: Peer Coaching to Strengthen Autism Support in Rural Schools ABSTRACT Rural schools often face limited access to evidence‐based autism services, making sustainable models of support essential. This study evaluated a peer‐coaching adaptation of the Collaborative Model for Promoting Competence and Success (COMPASS) to improve intervention implementation for students with autism in rural special education settings. Using a single‐case design, two teacher dyads, three students, and their caregivers participated in consultation and peer‐led coaching sessions focused on individualized social communication, engagement, and classroom participation goals. Goal attainment scaling (GAS) was used to monitor student progress. All students demonstrated improvement from baseline to intervention, with effect sizes indicating meaningful gains. Teachers and caregivers generally rated the peer‐coaching model as acceptable, though some teachers reported challenges related to limited time and competing responsibilities. Findings suggest that peer coaching may serve as a feasible, cost‐effective complement to consultation. title: School Disruption and Classroom Climate on Teachers’ Burnout and Wellbeing
text_snippet: School Disruption and Classroom Climate on Teachers’ Burnout and Wellbeing ABSTRACT Teachers with high levels of burnout and reduced levels of wellbeing are twice as likely to leave the teaching profession. For those that stay, it can result in strained relationships with their pupils and a difficulty to effectively manage classroom behavior. This study focused on the emotional strain felt by teachers during periods of educational disruption and how his varied according to school size, school‐level disadvantage and levels of pupil‐reported bullying and victimization. Data were collected from 11,111 primary school pupils and their 748 teachers in 2020 before the pandemic lockdowns, and in the summer of 2021 when schools had re‐opened. Teacher wellbeing and burnout levels (exhaustion, cynicism and professional efficacy) were collected. Teachers reported higher levels of burnout and reduced levels of wellbeing after the school disruption, and teachers of classrooms with the highest proportion of pupil bullying perpetration were found to have the lowest levels of teaching professional efficacy. title: A Study of the Impact of Emotion Regulation Support Program Applied to 60–72‐Month‐Old Children on Their Emotion Regulation Skills and Secure Base Relations With Their Teachers in Terms of Their Attachment Styles
text_snippet: A Study of the Impact of Emotion Regulation Support Program Applied to 60–72‐Month‐Old Children on Their Emotion Regulation Skills and Secure Base Relations With Their Teachers in Terms of Their Attachment Styles ABSTRACT The goal of this study is to analyze the impact of an Emotion Regulation Support Program applied to 60–72‐month‐old children on their emotion regulation skills and secure‐base relations with teachers in terms of their attachment styles. The study, carried out using a semi‐ intervention design with a pre‐test/post‐test and 1‐month follow‐up test design and a comparison group, included a study group of 100 children with secure, avoidant, and negative attachment styles (50 intervention group children, 50 children in the comparison group).
